transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-09-10 16:00 UTC | Duration 48m | Recording on.
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Ortega (Redwood SE), Amira Patel (VP Eng, Stratus), Benju Rao (Platform Lead), Olivia Park (Sec & Compliance).

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intro — I'm Maya, I'm the AE on this account, and Carlos is our SE who'll walk through the reliability specifics.
[00:12] Amira: Thanks Maya. We appreciate you making time; we've been evaluating hosted providers and also considering a private deployment for data residency. Big focus for us is incident tolerance and graceful degradation.
[00:25] Carlos: Great, Amira. High-level, we'll cover: multi-region routing, fallback policies when a region or model variant is unhealthy, SLA expectations, and operational playbooks — can tailor to your runbook. Is that the right agenda?
[00:36] Benju: Yes, exactly. Also curious about how Redwood handles prefix/KV cache across regions — cache warmup times matter for us.
[00:45] Olivia: And from my side, encryption at rest/in transit specifics, KMS integration and audit logs.
[00:52] Carlos: Understood. Quick question to orient capacity: what's your current peak QPS and tail-latency target?
[01:03] Benju: Peak is about 240 QPS across our EU+NA tiers. P95 generation latency we want under 350ms, and we can't have more than 0.5% errors over a rolling week.
[01:18] Maya: Perfect. That helps us recommend Hosted vs Dedicated. For 240 QPS with tight p95s, many customers go Dedicated to get predictable throughput — but there are tradeoffs.
[01:29] Amira: Can you outline the tradeoffs quickly? We want to understand cost and reliability differences.
[01:35] Carlos: Sure. Hosted gives rapid setup and automatic regional routing. We have multi-region endpoints and smart routing that uses health checks and policies — lowest latency or cost, or region-first routing. In failure scenarios, requests can failover to another region or a cheaper/quantized model variant. Dedicated gives isolated GPU pools and reserved capacity: lower jitter at high load, dedicated autoscaling policies, and capacity guarantees with SLAs. Private adds network isolation and on-prem control, but increases operational coordination and provisioning lead time.
[02:03] Amira: If an entire region goes down, what's the typical failover time?
[02:09] Carlos: For Hosted, with health checks and pre-warmed pools, you can expect cold failover to another region in the 5–30s ballpark depending on model KV cache size and prefix behavior. For Dedicated, if you replicate dedicated pools across two regions, failover can be sub-10s because we keep warmed caches and model variants active.
[02:27] Benju: That 5–30s range is wide — are there knobs to tune?
[02:33] Carlos: Yes. You can tune routing policies: synchronous failover vs async retry, keep-warm settings for key prefixes, and preloading KV cache. Also we support a hybrid where critical routes pin to dedicated pools in multiple regions to reduce warmup.
[02:47] Olivia: What about partial degradations — e.g., GPUs overloaded and tail latency spikes — how does Redwood degrade gracefully?
[02:57] Carlos: We have staged fallbacks: first, dynamic batching will adjust; second, automatic model-variant fallback — for example from fp16 to an 8-bit quantized variant that reduces latency but might slightly shift outputs; third, you can configure controlled rate limiting or circuit-breakers per customer or token. We also support soft-failures where we return cached completions for certain prompt templates while the model is recovering.
[03:21] Amira: Soft-failures sound interesting. How do you avoid quality regressions when falling back to quantized models?
[03:28] Carlos: We surface per-prompt eval scores and allow you to pin critical prompt families to stronger model variants. Our Optimize tooling can recommend which prompts are safe to serve on quantized variants based on historical evals.
[03:40] Maya: Also, we provide canary rollouts and A/B to test fallbacks in production with a small percentage of traffic before full switch.
[03:47] Benju: On KV cache — if we failover to a region without a warmed cache, do you reconstruct it from scratch? How long to get steady-state?
[03:57] Carlos: If KV isn't replicated, the second region will need to reconstruct caches. Warmup time depends on the effective context reuse in your workload; typical warmup to steady-state can be minutes under bursty traffic. We recommend replicating hot prefixes for critical routes. Replication is an optional configuration and is faster with Dedicated.
[04:16] Amira: Data residency — we cannot ship raw payloads outside EU for certain customers. Can Redwood route and keep processing strictly in-region?
[04:24] Carlos: Yes. We support region-only routing policies and dedicated instances in-region for Private or Dedicated. Hosted by default could route to nearest healthy region, but you can lock down a route to EU-only. For Private deployments we run inside your VPC so data never leaves your network.
[04:39] Olivia: For security we need KMS/HSM integration, SSO, and audit trails. Also proof of SOC2 and ISO.
[04:47] Maya: We'll send the Redwood security pack with SOC2 and ISO docs, plus details on KMS integrations and audit log retention options.
[04:55] Benju: Somebody mentioned cost of keeping multi-region warmed pools. How do we estimate that?
[05:03] Carlos: Cost is driven by reserved GPU hours for warm pools. If you provision active pools in two regions, cost roughly doubles for idle/warm capacity but gives much faster failover and lower tail latency. We can run a simulation with your traffic profile to estimate the cost/benefit.
[05:18] Amira: We need an error budget conversation too — what's Redwood's SLA and how do you measure it?
[05:25] Carlos: For Dedicated we offer SLA-backed uptime and latency targets — SLA specifics depend on the contract but a common template is 99.9% availability for the endpoint and P95 latency SLOs. Hosted has published uptime targets but dedicated SLAs are firmer. We measure from ingress to token-gen completion and ship token-level telemetry to the console for you to slice by route, model, and token.
[05:47] Benju: How are retries handled to avoid cascading overload during incidents?
[05:52] Carlos: We recommend client-side exponential backoff with jitter and server-side rate limiting. Redwood can enforce per-api-key quotas and token-rate throttles. We also support circuit breakers that short-circuit calls to fast-fail on downstream overload conditions to avoid cascading.
[06:09] Amira: Another concern — vendor lock-in. If we start on Hosted and later want Private, how hard is migration?
[06:17] Maya: We design the API and config layer to be consistent across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private. Model version pins, rollout policies, and routing config are portable. Data migration depends on whether you used Redwood-managed storage; for Private you'd bring own KMS and possibly replicate logs. We'll provide a migration checklist.
[06:34] Olivia: For compliance audits, we need immutable logs and per-request metadata. How long can logs be retained?
[06:41] Carlos: By default retention is 30 days in Hosted; enterprise plans allow longer retention (90d, 365d) or you can sink logs to your own archive (S3/GCS) — retention then matches your policy. We also support signed, immutable export streams for audit.
[06:58] Benju: Is there a recommended architecture for mission critical endpoints?
[07:03] Carlos: Yes — typical pattern: dual-region dedicated pools, pinned model versions, active-request routing with health checks, replicated hot-prefix cache, canary deployment gate, and a runbook with automated rollback thresholds. We can share a reference architecture diagram.
[07:20] Amira: Speaking of runbooks, can Redwood integrate with our PagerDuty and OpsGenie stack?
[07:26] Carlos: Absolutely. We emit alerts and webhook notifications; you can route to PagerDuty with severity mappings. We also surface incidents in the Console with trace IDs to speed up root-cause.
[07:36] Maya: Quick clarifying question — for the pilot what are the success criteria you want to use?
[07:41] Amira: We'll define success as: 1) Meet P95 <350ms for production-simulated workload, 2) No more than 0.5% error rate, 3) Demonstrate failover recovery within 30s with no data leakage, 4) Security checklist completed.
[07:55] Maya: Good. We'll align the pilot plan to those criteria.
[07:59] Benju: A practical question — when you fall back to quantized variants, do you surface a quality delta metric so we know which prompts are impacted?
[08:08] Carlos: Yes, we surface per-prompt regressions and we can tie alerts to a threshold. Optimize will recommend per-prompt serving surfaces.
[08:16] Olivia: On encryption and KMS — if we bring our own KMS, is key rotation managed by us?
[08:22] Carlos: You control key rotation. Redwood integrates with your KMS/HSM and we never see plaintext keys.
[08:27] Amira: Is there an example incident flow you can walk through, like region outage -> routing -> customer notify?
[08:34] Carlos: Sure: health checks detect latency/error spikes -> router shifts percent traffic away (can be immediate failover or staged) -> we initiate preconfigured fallback (model variant/region) -> console logs show impacted routes -> alert triggers PagerDuty and sends an annotated incident with traces -> runbook automated rollback if regression detected -> post-incident report with root cause and action items.
[09:00] Maya: I want to call out automatic fallback ordering is configurable — some customers prefer region-first, others prefer model-variant-first to avoid cross-region data movement.
[09:10] Benju: For us region-first is non-negotiable for certain customers.
[09:13] Carlos: You can set per-route policies to be region-only for sensitive traffic.
[09:19] Amira: Could you talk through a worst-case timeline — say a large region outage during peak traffic?
[09:26] Carlos: Worst case if you have a single-region setup: cold failover may cause increased latencies and partial errors while KV cache warms, with several minutes to steady-state. With dual-region dedicated pools and replicated hot-prefixes, failover is sub-10s and user impact minimal. The worst-case is if failover triggers model variant fallbacks that change output; hence the importance of canarying.
[09:50] Olivia: We need evidence for auditors that failovers are contained and logs show data did not leave EU. Can we get signed postmortems with provenance?
[09:59] Maya: Yes we'll include that in the security pack — we can provide signed attestations for pilot incidents and procedures for retained audit trails.
[10:07] Benju: From an ops perspective, what tooling will my platform team use day-to-day?
[10:12] Carlos: The Redwood Console. It shows per-route token cost, latency percentiles, traces, and a rollout manager to control canaries. There are also APIs for metrics and audit exports.
[10:22] Amira: When you say token-level telemetry, is that PII-safe? We have to scrub user identifiers before sending to Redwood in some flows.
[10:30] Carlos: You can choose sanitized payloads or redact fields client-side. For Private deployments you can also prevent Redwood control plane from receiving raw payloads entirely.
[10:40] Maya: Any other blockers from your side that would prevent starting a pilot?
[10:44] Amira: Need the security docs and pilot pricing. Also need the sample workload adapter for our integration team.
[10:50] Maya: We'll share the pack and a sample integration repo. Carlos, can you take the technical deep-dive?
[10:56] Carlos: Yep. I'll propose times next week.
[11:00] Benju: One more nit — in the console, can we mute autoscaling during a P0 incident to avoid unwanted spin-ups that could mask performance issues?
[11:09] Carlos: You can set autoscale policies and manual overrides. During incidents some customers set scaling to manual to observe behavior; we can template that into your runbook.
[11:18] Amira: For pilot duration, we want 3 months with a ramp to simulate peak. What's the minimum commitment for Dedicated?
[11:25] Maya: Typically monthly reserved for Dedicated, but we can do a short-term pilot with committed minimum for 3 months; pricing depends on GPU class and regions. I'll include a quote.
[11:34] Olivia: Will the pilot include security scanning and penetration testing?
[11:38] Maya: We can run a joint security testbed; standard scans are included and we can coordinate an external pentest if needed as an add-on.
[11:46] Carlos: Quick technical deep-dive note — for model-variant fallbacks we maintain compatibility by ensuring identical tokenizer and model schema; differences can still occur in outputs and we recommend baseline evals.
[11:57] Benju: Are there examples or case studies of other customers with similar constraints?
[12:02] Maya: We have a case study where a fintech customer ran dual-region dedicated pools and achieved sub-10s failover with <0.2% error spike during a major region outage. I'll share that link.
[12:13] Amira: That'd be helpful.
[12:17] Maya: Quick recap of action items then: I'll send security docs and pricing; Carlos will run routing simulation and schedule a technical deep-dive; Benju will share traffic profile. Anything else?
[12:29] Benju: That's it from us.
[12:31] Olivia: Thanks all.
[12:34] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials and proposed times.

[Post-call notes - automated summary may be imperfect]:
- Focus: Incident tolerance (failover time, graceful degradation), multi-region strategies, dedicated vs hosted tradeoffs, privacy/data residency, security controls.
- Pilot success criteria agreed: P95 <350ms, <0.5% error, failover within 30s, security checklist green.
- Potential risks: Cache-warmup delays during failover, cost for multi-region reserved capacity, model regressions when using quantized fallbacks, audit evidence for data residency.
- Reference artifacts to send: security pack (SOC2/ISO), runbook template, pilot quote, routing simulation results, case study links.

[End of transcript].
